paras: Real experience is expensive. Dyna-Q learns a one-step model from the transitions it sees, then between real steps it replays imagined transitions through that model, running extra Q-updates for free. A handful of planning steps per real step can slash the experience needed to solve a maze.
Each real step is followed by n planning updates on remembered transitions:
sections.texNote: More planning steps means faster learning - until the model's errors dominate.

sections.code:
model[s, a] = (r, s2)                  # learn the model
for _ in range(n):                    # plan
    (sp, ap), (rp, s2p) = sample(model)
    Q[sp, ap] += alpha * (rp + gamma * Q[s2p].max() - Q[sp, ap])
sections.caption: Act once, then imagine n more transitions.

takeaways: Dyna-Q mixes model-free learning with model-based planning.
Planning updates reuse a learned one-step model.
It is far more sample-efficient than model-free alone.

concepts.title: Generalized Advantage Estimation
concepts.oneLine: Tune the bias-variance trade-off of the advantage signal.

paras: Policy gradients need an advantage estimate: how much better was an action than expected? Use one-step TD and it is low-variance but biased by the critic; use the full return and it is unbiased but noisy. GAE blends all horizons with a decay lambda, giving a single knob to trade bias against variance.
An exponentially-weighted sum of TD residuals:
sections.texNote: lambda = 0 is one-step TD advantage; lambda = 1 is the Monte Carlo advantage.

sections.code:
adv, gae = np.zeros(T), 0.0
for t in reversed(range(T)):
    delta = r[t] + gamma * V[t+1] - V[t]
    gae = delta + gamma * lam * gae
    adv[t] = gae
sections.caption: A backward pass blends every horizon's TD error.

takeaways: GAE trades advantage bias against variance with lambda.
It is computed in one backward pass over a trajectory.
It is the standard advantage estimator inside PPO.

concepts.title: MDPs and the Bellman Equation
concepts.oneLine: Frame sequential decisions, and solve them with a recursive value identity.

paras: A Markov decision process is states, actions, rewards, and transitions. The value of a state is the best total reward you can expect from it. The Bellman equation makes this recursive: a state's value is the immediate reward plus the discounted value of where you land next - which value iteration solves by repeated backups.
The optimal value satisfies the Bellman optimality equation:
sections.texNote: gamma discounts the future; iterating this backup converges to V*.

sections.caption: Repeated backups converge to the optimal values.

takeaways: MDPs formalize sequential decision-making.
Bellman makes value recursive: reward now plus discounted value next.
Value iteration solves a known MDP by repeated backups.

concepts.title: Policy Gradients
concepts.oneLine: Optimize the policy directly by following the gradient of expected reward.

paras: Instead of learning values and acting greedily, policy gradients adjust the policy's parameters to make high-reward actions more likely. REINFORCE nudges the log-probability of each action by the return that followed it. It handles continuous actions naturally but can be high-variance.
The policy-gradient theorem weights each action's log-prob gradient by its return:
sections.texNote: Subtracting a baseline from G_t cuts variance without adding bias.

sections.code:
# REINFORCE update over a trajectory
for (s, a, G) in trajectory:
    grad = score(s, a)             # d log pi(a|s)/d theta
    theta += lr * grad * (G - baseline)
sections.caption: Make actions that led to high return more likely.

takeaways: Policy gradients optimize the policy directly.
REINFORCE scales each log-prob gradient by its return.
A baseline reduces variance without bias.

concepts.title: Proximal Policy Optimization
concepts.oneLine: Take the biggest safe policy step by clipping the update.

paras: Big policy-gradient steps can collapse a policy. PPO lets you reuse a batch for several updates but clips the change in action probabilities, so the new policy never strays too far from the old one. This simple clip makes training stable and sample-efficient - it is the default for RLHF.
Clip the probability ratio so the surrogate objective cannot reward going too far:
sections.texNote: r_t is the new/old probability ratio; outside the band the gradient is zero.

sections.code:
ratio = np.exp(logp_new - logp_old)
clip = np.clip(ratio, 1 - eps, 1 + eps)
loss = -np.minimum(ratio * A, clip * A).mean()
sections.caption: The clip parks the ratio inside a trust region.

takeaways: PPO clips the policy update into a trust region.
It allows several epochs per batch, stably.
It is the workhorse of modern RL and RLHF.

concepts.title: Q-Learning
concepts.oneLine: Learn action-values from experience, without knowing the environment.

paras: When you do not know the transition model, you learn from samples. Q-learning estimates the value of each action in each state, nudging its estimate toward the observed reward plus the best next-state value. It is off-policy: it learns the optimal policy even while exploring with a different one.
The temporal-difference update on the action-value Q:
sections.texNote: The bracket is the TD error - the surprise that drives learning.

sections.code:
td = r + gamma * Q[s2].max() - Q[s, a]
Q[s, a] += alpha * td
sections.caption: Move the estimate toward reward plus best next value.

takeaways: Q-learning is model-free, off-policy value learning.
The TD error is the learning signal.
max over next actions makes it learn the greedy optimum.

concepts.title: SARSA
concepts.oneLine: On-policy control: update toward the action you actually took.

paras: SARSA is Q-learning's on-policy twin. Where Q-learning bootstraps from the best next action, SARSA bootstraps from the action its policy actually chose next - so it learns the value of the policy it is following, exploration and all. On a cliff-edge task it learns the safe path; Q-learning learns the risky optimal one.
The target uses the next action a' sampled from the current policy:
sections.texNote: Replace Q(s',a') with max over a' and you are back to Q-learning.

sections.code:
a2 = policy(s2)                       # on-policy: sample next action
Q[s, a] += alpha * (r + gamma * Q[s2, a2] - Q[s, a])
sections.caption: Bootstrap from the action the policy really takes.

takeaways: SARSA is on-policy: it values the policy it follows.
Q-learning is off-policy: it values the greedy optimum.
On-policy learning is safer under exploration.

concepts.title: TD(lambda) and Eligibility Traces
concepts.oneLine: Dial smoothly between one-step TD and full Monte Carlo.

paras: One-step TD updates from the very next reward (low variance, biased); Monte Carlo waits for the full return (unbiased, high variance). TD(lambda) blends them with eligibility traces - a fading memory of recently visited states - so one update credits a whole trajectory. Intermediate lambda often learns fastest.
The trace decays by gamma*lambda and gates how much each state is updated:
sections.texNote: lambda = 0 is one-step TD; lambda = 1 is Monte Carlo.

sections.code:
delta = r + gamma * V[s2] - V[s]
e[s] += 1                              # mark visited
V += alpha * delta * e                 # update all eligible states
e *= gamma * lam                       # decay the trace
sections.caption: One TD error updates every recently-seen state.

takeaways: Eligibility traces credit a whole trajectory per step.
lambda interpolates TD(0) and Monte Carlo.
Intermediate lambda usually learns fastest.

concepts.title: Autograd and the Computational Graph
concepts.oneLine: How a framework records operations and replays them backward for gradients.

paras: PyTorch's autograd builds a graph as you compute: every tensor operation records its inputs and how to backpropagate through it. Calling .backward() walks that graph in reverse, applying the chain rule at each node, and deposits a gradient on every leaf tensor. You never write a derivative by hand.
Reverse-mode autodiff accumulates the gradient through each recorded op:
sections.texNote: Each op knows its local Jacobian-vector product; autograd chains them.

sections.code:
x = torch.tensor([2.0], requires_grad=True)
y = (x ** 2 + 3 * x).sum()
y.backward()          # walks the graph in reverse
print(x.grad)         # dy/dx = 2x + 3 = 7
sections.caption: Build the graph forward; differentiate it backward, automatically.

takeaways: Autograd records a graph of operations as you compute.
.backward() applies the chain rule in reverse over that graph.
Frameworks free you from writing derivatives by hand.

concepts.title: The Training Loop
concepts.oneLine: The five-line skeleton at the heart of every training script.

paras: Strip away the abstractions and every PyTorch training run is the same loop: get a batch, run the forward pass, compute the loss, backpropagate, and step the optimizer. Everything else - schedulers, logging, checkpoints, mixed precision - hangs off this skeleton.
Each iteration is one minibatch gradient-descent step:
sections.texNote: The minibatch B gives a noisy but cheap gradient estimate.

sections.code:
for x, y in loader:
    opt.zero_grad()
    loss = criterion(model(x), y)   # forward + loss
    loss.backward()                 # gradients
    opt.step()                      # update
sections.caption: Batch, forward, loss, backward, step - repeat.

takeaways: Every training script is this five-line loop.
Minibatches give cheap, noisy gradient estimates.
Schedulers, logging, and checkpoints decorate this skeleton.

concepts.title: The Optimizer Step
concepts.oneLine: How torch.optim turns accumulated gradients into a weight update.

paras: After backward fills in the gradients, an optimizer object applies the update rule. It holds the parameters and any per-parameter state (like Adam's moment estimates), and .step() applies the rule while .zero_grad() clears the gradients for the next iteration. Swapping SGD for Adam is a one-line change.
The optimizer applies its update rule to each parameter using its stored state:
sections.texNote: u is the rule (SGD, Adam, ...); state carries momentum and scale across steps.

sections.code:
opt = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=3e-4)
# each iteration:
opt.zero_grad()       # clear old grads
loss.backward()       # fill grads
opt.step()            # apply the update rule
sections.caption: zero_grad, backward, step - the same three calls every iteration.

takeaways: The optimizer owns the parameters and their update state.
.step() applies the rule; .zero_grad() resets gradients.
Changing optimizers is a one-line swap.

concepts.title: Gradient Clipping
concepts.oneLine: Cap the gradient norm so a bad batch cannot blow up training.

paras: Occasionally a batch produces a huge gradient that sends the weights flying and the loss to NaN - common in RNNs and transformers. Clipping rescales the gradient when its norm exceeds a threshold, preserving direction but bounding the step. Cheap insurance against rare instabilities.
Rescale the gradient if its norm exceeds the threshold c:
sections.texNote: Direction is preserved; only the magnitude is capped.

sections.caption: Keep the direction, bound the magnitude.

takeaways: Clipping bounds the update from a rare huge gradient.
It preserves direction, only scaling magnitude.
Standard practice for RNNs and transformers.

concepts.title: Learning-Rate Schedules
concepts.oneLine: Vary the step size over training - warm up, then decay.

paras: A fixed learning rate is a compromise. Schedules do better: a short warmup avoids early instability while statistics settle, then a decay (cosine or linear) lets the model settle into a good minimum. The right schedule can matter as much as the optimizer.
A cosine schedule decays smoothly from the peak rate to near zero:
sections.texNote: Often preceded by a linear warmup over the first few percent of steps.

sections.caption: Warm up, then cosine-decay to near zero.

takeaways: Schedules beat a single fixed learning rate.
Warmup avoids early divergence; decay sharpens the minimum.
Cosine decay is a strong default.

concepts.title: Mixed Precision
concepts.oneLine: Train in 16-bit for speed and memory, with safeguards for accuracy.

paras: Half-precision (fp16 / bf16) halves memory and runs far faster on modern hardware, but fp16's narrow range can underflow small gradients to zero. Mixed precision keeps a master copy of the weights in fp32 and scales the loss up before the backward pass so gradients stay representable, then scales them back down.
Loss scaling shifts gradients into fp16's representable range:
sections.texNote: Scale up by S before backward, unscale by S after - bf16's wider range often skips this.

sections.code:
scaled_loss = loss * S            # S ~ 2^14
scaled_loss.backward()
grads = [g / S for g in grads]    # unscale before the step
sections.caption: Compute in 16-bit, accumulate the master weights in 32-bit.

takeaways: fp16 / bf16 cut memory and speed up training.
Loss scaling stops fp16 gradients underflowing.
An fp32 master copy preserves accuracy.

concepts.title: Scaling Laws
concepts.oneLine: Loss falls as a predictable power law in compute, data, and parameters.

paras: Model quality improves smoothly and predictably with scale. Empirically, test loss drops as a power law in parameters, data, and compute - straight lines on a log-log plot. These curves let you forecast a big model's loss from small runs and allocate a compute budget optimally between size and data.
Loss versus a scale factor N follows a power law:
sections.texNote: Compute-optimal training (Chinchilla) balances N and data D for a fixed budget.

sections.code:
import numpy as np
# fit a power law to small-scale runs, extrapolate
logL = np.log(losses); logN = np.log(sizes)
slope, intercept = np.polyfit(logN, logL, 1)   # slope = -alpha
sections.caption: A line on a log-log plot predicts the next scale.

takeaways: Loss is a power law in compute, data, and parameters.
Small runs forecast large ones.
Compute-optimal training balances model size against data.

concepts.title: Knowledge Distillation
concepts.oneLine: Train a small student to mimic a big teacher's soft predictions.

paras: A big model's full probability distribution carries more information than a hard label - the relative scores of the wrong classes encode 'dark knowledge'. Distillation trains a small student to match the teacher's softened outputs, transferring much of the teacher's skill into a fraction of the size.
Match softened teacher and student distributions at temperature T:
sections.texNote: High T exposes the dark knowledge in the teacher's non-top classes.

sections.code:
soft_t = softmax(teacher_logits / T)
soft_s = softmax(student_logits / T)
loss = (1-a)*ce(y, student_logits) + a*T*T*kl(soft_t, soft_s)
sections.caption: Learn from the teacher's whole distribution, not just the label.

takeaways: Distillation transfers a teacher's soft predictions to a student.
Dark knowledge lives in the non-top class probabilities.
Temperature controls how much of it is exposed.

concepts.title: Mixture of Experts
concepts.oneLine: Route each token to a few specialist sub-networks, not all of them.

paras: A dense layer runs every parameter on every token. A mixture of experts has many expert sub-networks and a router that sends each token to just the top few. The model holds enormous total capacity, but each token only activates a slice of it - so quality scales with parameters while compute stays roughly fixed.
A router picks the top-k experts per token and mixes their outputs by gate weight:
sections.texNote: A load-balancing loss keeps the router from collapsing onto a few experts.

sections.code:
gate = softmax(router @ x)           # scores over experts
topk = gate.argsort()[-k:]           # pick k experts
y = sum(gate[e] * expert[e](x) for e in topk)
sections.caption: Only the top-k experts run per token.

takeaways: MoE activates only a few experts per token.
Total capacity grows while per-token compute stays fixed.
Load balancing prevents router collapse.

concepts.title: Paged Attention
concepts.oneLine: Manage the KV cache like virtual memory to kill fragmentation.

paras: Serving many requests with different lengths fragments the KV-cache memory, wasting much of the GPU. Paged attention borrows the OS idea of paging: store the cache in fixed-size blocks allocated on demand, so memory is packed tightly and sequences can share blocks. It is what lets servers batch far more requests.
A logical token position maps to a physical block and offset:
sections.texNote: Non-contiguous blocks via an indirection table - just like OS page tables.

sections.code:
# a block table maps logical positions to physical blocks
block = block_table[seq][i // B]
k = kv_blocks[block][i % B]            # gather K/V by page
sections.caption: Fixed-size pages, allocated on demand, packed tight.

takeaways: Paged attention pages the KV cache like virtual memory.
It removes fragmentation and packs more requests per GPU.
It is the core idea behind high-throughput servers like vLLM.

concepts.title: Pruning
concepts.oneLine: Remove the weights that barely matter to shrink the model.

paras: Most weights in a trained network contribute little. Magnitude pruning zeros the smallest ones, and a brief retrain lets the survivors compensate. Accuracy holds steady as sparsity rises, then falls off a cliff - the trick is finding that edge. Structured pruning removes whole channels for real speedups.
Keep only weights above a magnitude threshold:
sections.texNote: tau is set to hit a target sparsity; retrain after pruning to recover accuracy.

sections.code:
import numpy as np
thr = np.quantile(np.abs(W), sparsity)   # e.g. 0.8 -> drop 80%
W = W * (np.abs(W) > thr)                 # then fine-tune
sections.caption: Zero the small weights, retrain the rest.

takeaways: Pruning removes low-magnitude weights.
Accuracy holds then drops sharply past a sparsity edge.
Structured pruning yields real hardware speedups.

concepts.title: Quantization
concepts.oneLine: Store and compute weights in fewer bits with minimal accuracy loss.

paras: A model in 16-bit floats is mostly empty precision. Quantization maps weights to low-bit integers (8-bit, even 4-bit), shrinking memory and speeding up math. The trick is choosing a scale per group of weights so the rounding error stays small, and handling outliers that would otherwise stretch the scale.
Symmetric quantization rounds to a grid set by a per-group scale s:
sections.texNote: Smaller groups and outlier handling keep the reconstruction error low.

sections.caption: Round to a grid; dequantize by multiplying back.

takeaways: Quantization trades precision for memory and speed.
Per-group scales keep rounding error small.
Outliers are the main accuracy challenge.

concepts.title: Speculative Decoding
concepts.oneLine: Draft several tokens with a small model, verify them with the big one.

paras: Generation is slow because the big model runs once per token. Speculative decoding has a cheap draft model propose several tokens at once; the big model then checks them all in a single parallel pass and accepts the longest correct prefix. It is exactly as accurate as the big model, just faster.
Accept a drafted token with a probability that preserves the target distribution:
sections.texNote: A correction step on rejection makes the output identical in distribution to the target.

sections.code:
draft = small.generate(ctx, k=4)           # propose k tokens
p = big.logprobs(ctx, draft)               # verify in one pass
accept = longest_prefix_where(p_ratio >= u) # keep correct prefix
sections.caption: Propose cheaply, verify in parallel, keep the correct prefix.

takeaways: Speculative decoding drafts cheap, verifies expensive.
Output is identical in distribution to the big model.
Speedup depends on how often drafts are accepted.

concepts.title: Guardrails
concepts.oneLine: Filter inputs and outputs to keep an LLM system safe.

paras: A deployed model needs a safety pipeline around it. Input guards strip or flag prompt injection and sensitive data; output guards catch unsafe content, leaked secrets, or off-policy responses before they reach the user. Each guard is a focused check; turning one off lets the matching threat through.
The system passes only if every guard passes:
sections.texNote: Layered, independent checks - defense in depth, not a single classifier.

sections.code:
def guarded(prompt):
    if injection(prompt) or has_pii(prompt): return BLOCK
    out = model(sanitize(prompt))
    if toxic(out) or leaks_secret(out): return BLOCK
    return out
sections.caption: Check the input, generate, then check the output.

takeaways: Guardrails wrap the model with input and output checks.
Layered, independent guards give defense in depth.
Removing a guard exposes exactly its threat class.

concepts.title: HyDE
concepts.oneLine: Retrieve with a hypothetical answer instead of the raw question.

paras: A question and its answer often look different in embedding space, so querying with the question can miss the right passage. HyDE first has the model write a hypothetical answer, embeds that, and retrieves with it - because a guessed answer, even if imperfect, sits much closer to the real supporting documents.
Retrieve against the embedding of a generated answer h, not the query q:
sections.texNote: Averaging several hypothetical answers smooths out any single bad guess.

sections.code:
h = llm(f'Write a passage answering: {q}')   # hypothetical doc
hits = vector_search(embed(h), k=5)          # retrieve with it
sections.caption: Guess an answer, retrieve what supports it.

takeaways: HyDE bridges the query-document embedding gap.
It retrieves with a generated answer, not the question.
Averaging multiple drafts reduces variance.

concepts.title: Prompt Injection
concepts.oneLine: The attacks that hijack an LLM, and the layered defenses against them.

paras: Because an LLM cannot fully separate instructions from data, attacker-controlled text - in a prompt, a retrieved document, or a tool result - can override your instructions. Defenses layer up: delimit and spotlight untrusted content, assert an instruction hierarchy, classify inputs, and filter outputs for exfiltration. No single layer is sufficient.
Residual risk is what survives every defense layer:
sections.texNote: ASR is attack success rate; each defense d_l catches some fraction, none all.

sections.code:
# spotlighting: clearly fence untrusted content
prompt = (system + '
<<UNTRUSTED>>
' + retrieved + '
<<END>>')
# plus an output filter that blocks secret/exfiltration patterns
sections.caption: Defense in depth - delimit, prioritize, classify, filter.

takeaways: Injection exploits the instruction-vs-data ambiguity.
Untrusted text can arrive via documents and tool results.
Layered defenses reduce, but never zero, the attack surface.

concepts.title: Chunking for Retrieval
concepts.oneLine: Split documents so the answer survives retrieval intact.

paras: Retrieval-augmented generation grounds a model in your documents - but only if the right passage is retrievable. Chunking decides how documents are split into embeddable units. Too large and a chunk dilutes the relevant sentence; too small and it loses context. Overlap and sentence-aware boundaries keep answers from being cut in half.
Retrieve the top chunks by similarity to the query embedding:
sections.texNote: Chunk size and overlap control whether the answer span lands inside one retrieved chunk.

sections.caption: Sliding windows with overlap keep answer spans whole.

takeaways: Chunking sets what retrieval can actually find.
Size and overlap trade context against precision.
Sentence-aware splits avoid cutting answers in half.

concepts.title: The ReAct Agent Loop
concepts.oneLine: Interleave reasoning with tool calls in a thought-action-observation loop.

paras: A ReAct agent alternates thinking and acting: it reasons about what to do, calls a tool, observes the result, and repeats until it can answer. Tools (search, a calculator, code) let it ground its reasoning in real results instead of hallucinating - but every step is a chance to go off the rails, so reliability compounds.
End-to-end success is the product of per-step reliability:
sections.texNote: Many steps at 0.9 each still fail often - hence verification and retries.

sections.code:
while not done:
    thought = model(scratchpad)            # reason
    action, arg = parse_tool(thought)      # act
    obs = tools[action](arg)               # observe
    scratchpad += f'{thought}\n{obs}\n'
sections.caption: Thought, action, observation - loop until answered.

takeaways: ReAct interleaves reasoning with grounded tool calls.
Tools curb hallucination by injecting real results.
Per-step error compounds, so reliability is the hard part.

concepts.title: Reflection
concepts.oneLine: Draft, critique, and revise toward a quality bar.

paras: A model can often improve its own output if asked to critique it. Reflection loops draft -> critique -> revise until a quality bar is met. The catch: self-correction is only as good as the critic. A sharp critic converges fast; a weak or miscalibrated one can pass bad answers or reject good ones.
Quality improves only when the critic carries real signal:
sections.texNote: Bounded by the verifier: a useless critic yields no gain.

sections.code:
draft = llm(task)
for _ in range(max_iters):
    critique = llm(f'Critique: {draft}')
    if passes(critique): break
    draft = llm(f'Revise given: {critique}\n{draft}')
sections.caption: Iterate until the critic is satisfied - or you give up.

takeaways: Reflection is a draft-critique-revise loop.
Its ceiling is the quality of the critic.
It is the sequential cousin of self-consistency.

concepts.title: Reranking
concepts.oneLine: Re-score the top retrieved hits with a more careful model.

paras: Fast vector search uses a bi-encoder that embeds query and document separately - cheap but coarse. A reranker is a cross-encoder that reads the query and a candidate together, scoring relevance far more accurately. You retrieve many cheaply, then rerank the top few expensively: the best of both.
A cross-encoder scores the query-document pair jointly:
sections.texNote: Joint encoding captures interactions a separate-embedding bi-encoder misses.

sections.code:
cands = vector_search(q, k=50)          # cheap recall
scores = [cross_encoder(q, d) for d in cands]
top = [cands[i] for i in argsort(scores)[::-1][:5]]
sections.caption: Retrieve broadly, rerank the shortlist precisely.

takeaways: Bi-encoders retrieve fast; cross-encoders rerank accurately.
Retrieve many, rerank a few - the standard two-stage pipeline.
Reranking sharply improves the final context quality.

concepts.title: Self-Consistency
concepts.oneLine: Sample several reasoning paths and take the majority answer.

paras: A single chain of reasoning can go wrong by chance. Self-consistency samples several independent chains at nonzero temperature and votes on the final answer. When errors are independent, the majority is far more reliable than any one path - a Condorcet-style lift. It fails when the errors are correlated.
With independent per-sample accuracy p, the majority of N improves sharply:
sections.texNote: Correlated errors break the independence this relies on.

sections.code:
from collections import Counter
answers = [extract(llm(prompt, temperature=0.7)) for _ in range(N)]
final = Counter(answers).most_common(1)[0][0]   # vote
sections.caption: Many samples, one vote - reliability from diversity.

takeaways: Self-consistency votes over multiple reasoning samples.
Independent errors make the majority much more reliable.
Correlated errors defeat it.

concepts.title: Calibration
concepts.oneLine: Make a model's confidence match its real accuracy.

paras: A trustworthy classifier that says 90% should be right about 90% of the time. Modern networks are often overconfident. Calibration fixes the scores without changing the ranking - temperature scaling divides the logits by a single learned constant so the confidences line up with observed accuracy.
Temperature scaling softens the logits by a learned scalar T:
sections.texNote: T > 1 reduces overconfidence; it is fit on validation data and leaves the argmax unchanged.

sections.code:
# fit T to minimize validation NLL; predictions unchanged in rank
p = softmax(logits / T)
ece = expected_calibration_error(p, labels)
sections.caption: One scalar recalibrates every confidence.

takeaways: Calibration aligns confidence with actual accuracy.
Temperature scaling fixes it with a single constant.
It changes confidences but not the predicted class.

concepts.title: Conformal Prediction
concepts.oneLine: Output prediction sets with a guaranteed coverage rate.

paras: Instead of one guess, conformal prediction returns a set that contains the truth with a chosen probability - say 90% - and that guarantee holds for any model, with no distributional assumptions. When the model is unsure the set is large; when it is confident the set shrinks. It turns any predictor into one with honest uncertainty.
Use a calibration quantile of nonconformity scores to build the set:
sections.texNote: Coverage of at least 1 - alpha holds marginally; set size grows as the model weakens.

sections.code:
import numpy as np
scores = nonconformity(calib_X, calib_y)
qhat = np.quantile(scores, 1 - alpha)        # threshold
pred_set = [y for y in classes if score(x, y) <= qhat]
sections.caption: Calibrate a threshold; include every plausible label.

takeaways: Conformal sets guarantee coverage for any model.
Set size grows when the model is uncertain.
Coverage is distribution-free and finite-sample valid.

concepts.title: Fairness Metrics
concepts.oneLine: Measure group disparities - and confront their impossibility.

paras: A model can be accurate yet unfair across groups. Different metrics formalize fairness: demographic parity (equal positive rates), equal opportunity (equal true-positive rates), equalized odds (both error rates equal). The uncomfortable result is that, when base rates differ, you cannot satisfy them all at once - fairness requires a choice.
Equal opportunity demands matched true-positive rates across groups:
sections.tex: P(\hat{y}=1\mid y=1, A=a) = P(\hat{y}=1\mid y=1, A=b)
sections.texNote: Demographic parity and calibration generally cannot hold simultaneously with this.

sections.code:
tpr = lambda g: ((pred==1) & (y==1) & (A==g)).sum() / ((y==1)&(A==g)).sum()
eo_gap = abs(tpr('a') - tpr('b'))      # equal-opportunity gap
sections.caption: Compute per-group rates; the gaps are the disparities.

takeaways: Fairness has several incompatible definitions.
With unequal base rates you cannot satisfy them all.
Choosing a metric is a value judgment, not a technicality.

concepts.title: Time-Series Forecasting
concepts.oneLine: Predict future values from the patterns in past observations.

paras: Forecasting exploits structure in time: trend, seasonality, and autocorrelation. Classical methods decompose the series and extrapolate; modern ones learn the patterns directly. The cardinal rule is to respect time when you evaluate - never let the model peek at the future, and backtest on rolling windows.
A series is often modeled as trend plus seasonality plus noise:
sections.texNote: Validate with rolling-origin backtests, never a random split.

sections.caption: Beat this baseline before trusting anything fancier.

takeaways: Forecasting models trend, seasonality, and autocorrelation.
Evaluate with rolling backtests, never a random split.
Always compare against a seasonal-naive baseline.

concepts.title: Explainability with SHAP
concepts.oneLine: Attribute a prediction fairly across its input features.

paras: Why did the model decide this? SHAP answers by borrowing from game theory: treat features as players and the prediction as a payout, then give each feature its Shapley value - its average marginal contribution across all orderings. It is the unique attribution that is fair and adds up to the prediction.
The Shapley value averages a feature's marginal contribution over all coalitions:
sections.texNote: The contributions sum exactly to the prediction minus the baseline.

sections.code:
# exact Shapley by enumerating coalitions (small feature sets)
from itertools import combinations
# phi_i = average of f(S + i) - f(S) over all subsets S not containing i
sections.caption: Average marginal contribution over every feature ordering.

takeaways: SHAP gives each feature its fair share of the prediction.
Attributions sum to the prediction minus a baseline.
It is the game-theoretic standard for local explanations.

concepts.title: Autoscaling
concepts.oneLine: Track demand by adding and removing replicas automatically.

paras: Traffic rises and falls; a fixed fleet either wastes money or breaks under load. An autoscaler watches a signal like utilization and adjusts the replica count toward a target. The catch is cold starts: new replicas take time to warm up, so spikes can breach the SLO before capacity catches up.
The desired replica count chases the load toward a target utilization:
sections.texNote: Lower target utilization buys headroom for spikes, at higher cost.

sections.code:
desired = ceil(load / (target_util * cap_per_replica))
replicas = clamp(desired, min_r, max_r)   # cold start adds lag
sections.caption: Scale toward a utilization target, bounded by limits.

takeaways: Autoscaling matches replicas to demand.
Target utilization trades headroom against cost.
Cold starts cause SLO breaches on sudden spikes.

concepts.title: Canary Rollouts
concepts.oneLine: Ship a new model to a slice of traffic, watch, then ramp or roll back.

paras: Deploying a new model to everyone at once is risky. A canary sends a small fraction of traffic to the new version, compares its error rate against the old one with a statistical test, and only ramps up if it passes. A regression hits a few percent of users instead of all of them, and rolls back automatically.
A one-sided test gates each ramp stage on the error-rate difference:
sections.texNote: Pass the guard, ramp the traffic split; fail, roll back.

sections.caption: Ramp the split only while the guard holds.

takeaways: Canaries limit a bad deploy's blast radius.
A statistical guard decides ramp versus rollback.
Progressive traffic shifting makes releases safe.

concepts.title: Drift Detection
concepts.oneLine: Notice when production data has shifted away from training.

paras: Models silently decay when the world changes - new user behavior, a shifted input distribution, a broken upstream feature. Drift detection compares the live input distribution against a training reference and raises an alarm when they diverge, so you retrain before accuracy quietly collapses.
The population stability index sums the binned distribution shift:
sections.texNote: PSI above ~0.2 flags a meaningful shift worth investigating.

sections.caption: Bin both distributions; sum the divergence.

takeaways: Drift detection compares live data to a training reference.
PSI quantifies distribution shift; ~0.2 is a common alarm.
Catching drift early triggers retraining before accuracy falls.

concepts.title: Serving and Batching
concepts.oneLine: Trade a little latency for far more throughput by batching requests.

paras: A served model spends most of its time idle between requests. Dynamic batching waits a few milliseconds to gather several requests and runs them together, amortizing the fixed cost and multiplying throughput. The knob is the batch window: bigger batches mean higher throughput but more tail latency.
By Little's law, queue length ties throughput to latency:
sections.texNote: Push arrival rate lambda past capacity and the queue - and latency W - runs away.

sections.code:
# accumulate until full or the window elapses, then run once
batch = collect(max_size=32, max_wait_ms=5)
results = model(batch)        # one padded forward for many requests
sections.caption: Wait briefly, batch, run once - amortize the fixed cost.

takeaways: Batching amortizes fixed cost into higher throughput.
The batch window trades throughput against tail latency.
Arrivals past capacity make the queue run away.
